ety.text: From Middle English oure, from Old English ūre, ūser (“our”), from Proto-Germanic *unseraz (“of us, our”), from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-s-ero- (“our”). Cognate with Scots oor (“our”), West Frisian ús (“our”), Low German uns (“our”), Dutch onze (“our”), German unser, unsere (“our”) Danish vor (“our”), Norwegian vår (“our”), and more distantly Latin noster.

senses.d: Belonging to us, excluding the person(s) being addressed (exclusive our).
ex: Sorry, you're not invited to our party.
Paying no attention to Lizzy, Mrs. Gibson began calling out our names in alphabetical order.

senses.d: Belonging to us, including the person(s) being addressed (inclusive our).
ex: We must try to save our marriage for the sake of our children.

senses.d: Of, from, or belonging to any entity that the speaker is a part of or identifies with, such as place of employment or education, nation, region, language, etc.
ex: Our safety record at ABC Widgets is very good.
In English, our nouns do not generally have gender.

senses.d: Belonging to people in general.
ex: As we get older, our reactions get slower.

senses.d: Belonging to everyone being addressed.
ex: How are we all tonight? Have we got our happy faces on?

senses.d: Belonging to an individual being addressed; used especially of a person in the speaker's care, or to whom advice or instruction is being given.
ex: How are we feeling this morning, Mrs Miggins? Have we taken our tablets yet?
You've been spending all your money boozing when you have a wife and family to support. I think we need to get our priorities straight.

senses.d: Belonging to a third person, especially someone in the speaker's care.
ex: "I've just been to see Mrs Miggins." — "And how is she?" — "Not too good today. We've had a little problem with our tummy."

senses.d: Used to imply connection between the speaker's experiences or activities and a group of listeners.
ex: Hey guys, in this video I'll show you how I make my upside-down sponge cake. First, let's get our ingredients weighed out.

senses.d: Used before a person's name to indicate that the person is in one's family, or is a very close friend.
ex: I'm going to see our Terry for tea.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French nostre, from Latin noster.
Inherited from Old Spanish nuestro, Latin nostrum, from Proto-Italic *nosteros.

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese nosso, from Latin nostrum (“our”), from Proto-Italic *nosteros.

phr: I'll go to the foot of our stairs

ety.text: From Middle English oures, attested since the 1300s. Equivalent to our + -s (compare -'s); formed by analogy to his. Displaced ourn (from Middle English ouren) in standard speech.

senses.d: Excluding the person(s) being addressed (exclusive ours)
ex: You can't take that! It's ours!
Could we ask you to move, please. These seats are ours.

senses.d: Including the person(s) being addressed (inclusive ours).
ex: We should ask for it back. After all, it is ours.
Don't you think that ours looks much nicer than theirs?

senses.d: That or those belonging to any entity that the speaker is a part of or identifies with, such as place of employment or education, nation, region, language, etc.
ex: French food is better than ours.

senses.d: That or those belonging to people in general.
ex: As we get older, maintaining an active social life should be a priority of ours.

senses.d: That or those belonging to everyone being addressed.
ex: Good evening everyone. How are we all tonight? I know I've got my happy face on; have we all got ours on too?

senses.d: That or those belonging to an individual being addressed; used especially to a person in the speaker's care, or to whom advice or instruction is being given.
ex: Hello Mrs Miggins. How are we feeling this morning? Oh, what's that bottle of tablets under our chair? Is that ours?

senses.d: Used to imply connection between the speaker's experiences or activities and a group of listeners.
ex: Hey guys, in this video I'll show you how I make my upside-down sponge cake. There are lots of recipes for these, but ours is the best.

senses.d: Our house or home.
ex: You can stay the night at ours if you like.

senses.d: Us; the group including the speaker as the object of a verb or preposition when that group also is the subject.
ex: We should keep this for ourselves.
Let's not beat ourselves up over this.

senses.d: Intensifies the subject as the group including the speaker, especially to indicate that no one else satisfies the predicate or needs to be included.
ex: We did it ourselves.

senses.d: Referring to everyone being addressed.
ex: Come on everyone! Let's get ourselves up and out of bed, please.
Now then children, I'm not going to help you with the next problem. We should be able to work this one out ourselves.

senses.d: Referring to an individual person being addressed, especially a person in the speaker's care; also ourself.
ex: Coordinate term: nurse's we
Hello Mrs Miggins. Did we manage to wash ourselves this morning?

ety.text: Uncertain. Rohlfs and Von Wartburg favoured Late Latin ecce hīc. Maiden casts doubt on this etymology, pointing out that Italian ci is an unstressed 'weak' form, while Latin hic otherwise survives in Italian only in stressed forms (reinforced by Latin ecce or eccum) such as ciò, qua, and qui.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish nos (“us”) (from Latin nōs) + otros (“others”) (plural of otro, from Latin alter). Compare Galician nosoutros, Catalan nosaltres, Occitan nosautres, French nous autres, Friulian noaltris, Italian noialtri.
